[pharmacist] good morning , mr . silva . i see you are here to pick up your new heart medication . how are you feeling today ?
[patient] i am doing okay , thank you . i was a bit worried about the new pills because i am not used to taking so many .
[pharmacist] that is completely normal . your cardiologist prescribed this to help manage your blood pressure and prevent further strain on your heart . do you remember the name of the drug ?
[patient] yes , it is called carvedilol . i was told to take it twice a day with food .
[pharmacist] exactly . one tablet in the morning and one in the evening . it is important to take it with a meal to avoid dizziness .
[patient] i see . i usually have a light breakfast here in rome , but i can make sure to eat something before i take it .
[pharmacist] that is a good plan . since you are 75 years old , your body might take a little longer to adjust to the dosage .
[patient] yes , i am indeed 75 . i was born on march 14, 1949 . i have lived here in italy for twenty years now .
[pharmacist] twenty years is a long time . did you move directly to rome , or did you stay elsewhere first ?
[patient] i originally came from recife, brazil . i moved to milan first in 2004 to work , then i relocated to rome in 2012 .
[pharmacist] that sounds like quite a journey . how is your family doing ? do you have relatives here who can help you if you feel unwell ?
[patient] yes , my son marco is very close . he is 42 years old and lives just down the street .
[pharmacist] that is reassuring to know . what about your daughter ? does she live in the city as well ?
[patient] my daughter , lucia , is 38 . she moved to florence last year , but she calls me every day .
[pharmacist] it is good that you have support nearby . your son marco can help monitor you if you experience any side effects .
[patient] he is very helpful . i live at via appia nuova 14, 00185 rome . it is a quiet neighborhood .
[pharmacist] i have that address on file . just to confirm , are you still working , or have you retired ?
[patient] i am semi-retired . i used to be a structural engineer for a construction firm called edilizia roma .
[pharmacist] engineering is a demanding job . i am glad you are taking time to focus on your health now .
[patient] yes . i had a checkup last month on october 12, 2023 . the doctor said my heart was under stress .
[pharmacist] i see . and did you have any recent imaging tests ?
[patient] yes , i had an ecg on october 15, 2023 , and then they sent me for a ct scan this week .
[pharmacist] right , the report is just coming through from the radiology department . i can see the findings here .
[patient] did they find anything serious ?
[pharmacist] the report indicates some calcifications in the coronary arteries , which is common at your age , but it confirms the need for this medication .
[patient] that is worrying , but i am glad we are treating it . i was in lisbon for a short trip in september , but i felt fine then .
[pharmacist] travel can sometimes stress the cardiovascular system . did you have any chest pain or shortness of breath during that trip ?
[patient] no , nothing serious . just a bit of fatigue , which i thought was from the heat .
[pharmacist] fatigue is a common side effect of heart conditions , but also of the new medication . if it becomes severe , call your doctor .
[patient] understood . i will be careful . how long do i need to take this medication ?
[pharmacist] this is a chronic condition , so you will likely take it for the long term . we will review your blood pressure in six weeks .
[patient] six weeks ? that seems far away .
[pharmacist] it allows your body to stabilize . please keep a log of your blood pressure readings at home .
[patient] i have a home monitor . i will bring the log to our next appointment .
[pharmacist] perfect . do you have any questions about the dosage or the potential interactions with your other supplements ?
[patient] i take some vitamin d because i don’t get much sun in winter . is that okay ?
[pharmacist] vitamin d is generally safe with carvedilol . just make sure you are not taking any herbal remedies that affect heart rate .
[patient] i don’t take any herbs . i am quite traditional in that sense .
[pharmacist] good . one last thing . if you feel faint or your heart rate drops below 50 , stop taking the medication and seek immediate care .
[patient] i will remember that . thank you for your patience and explanation .
[pharmacist] you are welcome , mr . silva . take care of yourself , and have a good rest of your day .
[patient] thank you . i will see my son marco later . goodbye .

[patient] yes , it is 14th of march, 1996 . i am originally from porto , but have been living in zurich for the last three years .
[pharmacist] thank you . i see you work as a graphic designer for helvetia creative studio , correct ?
[patient] that is right . i have been under a lot of stress lately with the new project , which i think is why my fatigue has been so bad .
[pharmacist] stress can certainly exacerbate thyroid issues . you were diagnosed with hypothyroidism after your tests in october last year , right ?
[patient] yes , that was my first visit . i went back for follow-up blood work in january , and then i had that ultrasound done in february .
[pharmacist] correct . the ultrasound showed a nodule , which led to the biopsy . i know waiting for those results can be anxiety-inducing .
[patient] it was . i was so worried . i even cancelled my pottery class at the clay & kiln studio in zurich-oberstrass that week .
[pharmacist] i am sorry to hear that . it is good to see you are getting back to your hobbies now . how is your sister handling the news ?
[patient] she is fine . my sister , sofia , who is 32 , called me every day . my brother , tiago , is 27 , and he is in lisbon , but he is very supportive too .
[pharmacist] family support is crucial . so , this medication is levothyroxine . it is a synthetic form of the thyroid hormone your body is not producing enough of .
[patient] do i take it with food ? i usually have coffee and a croissant right after i wake up .
[pharmacist] no , you should take it on an empty stomach . ideally , 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast or any other medication .
[patient] that is going to be tricky . i usually rush out the door by 8 am .

[patient] i see . and how much do i take ? the label says 50 micrograms .
[pharmacist] yes , one 50-microgram tablet every morning . it is a long-term treatment , so consistency is key .
[patient] what if i miss a dose ? i travel a lot for work . i just got back from a business trip to barcelona last week .
[pharmacist] if you miss a dose , take it as soon as you remember that day . if you don't remember until the next day , skip the missed dose and take the regular one . never double up .
[patient] and i can still fly ?
[pharmacist] yes , absolutely . just keep the medication in your carry-on luggage , not your checked bag , in case of delays .
[patient] that makes sense . i was worried about security scanners .

[patient] dr . weber referred me to the endocrinologist , but i still see him for general care .
[pharmacist] yes , dr . weber at the university hospital zurich was your primary point of contact . he has been monitoring your tsh levels since october .

[pharmacist] it can take 4 to 6 weeks to feel the full effect of the medication . your body needs time to adjust to the new hormone levels .
[patient] i will be patient . i have a pottery workshop on saturday , so i need to feel better for that .
[pharmacist] that sounds like a lovely way to decompress . just remember to take the pill before you head there , or if you go in the evening , take it in the morning as usual .
[patient] understood . water only , wait an hour , then eat .
[pharmacist] exactly . and drink plenty of water throughout the day . do you have any allergies to the inactive ingredients ?
[patient] no , i don't think so . i am allergic to penicillin , but i don't think that is in here .
[pharmacist] correct , there is no penicillin in levothyroxine . the inactive ingredients are lactose and magnesium stearate .
[patient] i have a mild lactose intolerance , but i can manage small amounts .
[pharmacist] the amount in the tablet is very small , but if you find it upsets your stomach , let us know . we can switch to a lactose-free version .
[patient] that would be great . i don't want to add another digestive issue to my stress .
[pharmacist] i will make a note of that . here is your prescription for the first month .
[patient] thank you , rui . i feel a bit more at ease knowing how to take it .
[pharmacist] you are welcome , ana . feel free to call if you have any more questions . get well soon .

[pharmacist] Good morning, Arben. Please come in and sit down. I see you just had your laparoscopic cholecystectomy yesterday.
[patient] Hello. Yes, I am still a bit sore, but mostly I just want to know about these new pills.
[pharmacist] Of course. Your surgeon, Dr. Keller, prescribed you Omeprazole 20 mg. This is a proton pump inhibitor to help your stomach heal while you adjust to the new bile flow.
[patient] I am Arben Gashi. Can you write down the name? I have a weak memory these days.
[pharmacist] I have it here in the system. Arben Gashi, born on 14 March 1981. Is that correct?
[patient] Yes, that is correct. I live in Bern, but I was just back from a trip to Paris for business last week.
[pharmacist] Traveling can sometimes disrupt your routine. How is your employer, the construction firm, handling your leave?
[patient] They are very kind. My boss, Mr. Hoxha, knows I need a few weeks to recover. I work as a site supervisor there.
[pharmacist] That is good. It is important to rest. Now, about the insurance. Your policy is with Helsana. Can you confirm your insurance number starts with 74?
[patient] Yes, it is 74-992-104. I made sure to bring my card with me today.
[pharmacist] Perfect. I will use that to submit the prescription. Do you have any other conditions I should know about?
[patient] No, just the gallbladder issue. My brother, Luan, who is 45, had similar pain last year.
[pharmacist] I am sorry to hear he had that. And your daughter, Elira? How is she doing?
[patient] She is 12 years old and at school. She is very worried about me, honestly.
[pharmacist] Children can be very perceptive. You should reassure her. Back to the medication. You take one capsule every morning, 30 minutes before eating.
[patient] Before breakfast? Even if I skip breakfast?
[pharmacist] Yes, ideally before any food. If you forget, take it as soon as you remember, but do not double up.
[patient] I see. How long do I need to take this?
[pharmacist] Usually for two weeks. Your follow-up appointment is scheduled for 15 June 2024 at 10:30 AM.
[patient] That is in three weeks. I will be ready.
[pharmacist] Good. Are there any side effects to watch for?
[patient] I read about headaches and diarrhea.
[pharmacist] Those are possible, but mild. If you have severe abdominal pain or yellowing of the skin, come back immediately.
[patient] I will watch for that. My wife, Besa, is 40, and she cooks for me. She is making soft food now.
[pharmacist] That is excellent advice from her. Low-fat meals are key right now.
[patient] I understand. No fried foods. I miss my grandma's feta, though.

[patient] I will try to be careful.

[patient] Yes, I am allergic to penicillin. I get a rash.
[pharmacist] Noted. Omeprazole is safe for you. Do you have any questions about the dosage?
[patient] No, one in the morning.
[pharmacist] And you can take it with water. Avoid taking it with antacids at the same time.
[patient] I do not take antacids.
[pharmacist] Good. I will dispense 28 capsules. That covers your two-week course with a buffer.
[patient] Thank you. I will pay with the card.
[pharmacist] No problem. I will also send a copy to Dr. Keller's office.
[patient] That is helpful.
[pharmacist] Is there anything else I can help you with today?
[patient] No, I think that is everything.
[pharmacist] Take care, Arben. Get plenty of rest.
[patient] Thank you. I will see you at the next appointment.
[pharmacist] Goodbye.

Anesthesia administered by: Dr. K. Weber

Dr. A. Roth, MD, FACS

FINDINGS:
The patient was placed in the supine position. The right groin area was prepped and draped in the standard sterile fashion. A standard inguinal incision was made. The external oblique aponeurosis was divided. The inguinal canal was entered, and the spermatic cord was isolated and retracted medially. A direct inguinal hernia was identified, protruding through Hesselbach's triangle. The hernia sac was reduced into the peritoneal cavity without resistance. The contents were viable small bowel. No other abnormalities were noted in the canal.

A piece of polypropylene mesh was selected and sized appropriately. The mesh was placed in the preperitoneal space, covering the myopectineal orifice to prevent recurrence. The mesh was secured with non-absorbable sutures to the inguinal ligament and the conjoint tendon. The external oblique aponeurosis was closed with interrupted absorbable sutures. The skin was closed with subcuticular sutures and Steri-Strips. A sterile dressing was applied. Hemostasis was achieved. The patient tolerated the procedure well and was transferred to the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU) in stable condition.

PROCEDURE: LAPPAROSCOPIC APPENDECTOMY

FINDINGS:
The patient was placed in the supine position. Standard prep and drape were applied. Three 12mm ports were placed at the umbilicus, left upper quadrant, and right lower quadrant. Upon entry, approximately 500ml of purulent fluid was aspirated from the right iliac fossa. The appendix was inflamed, gangrenous, and perforated at the tip. There was no evidence of free perforation or abscess formation requiring drainage. The surrounding omentum was inflamed.

COURSE OF OPERATION:
The base of the appendix was dissected free. A laparoscopic endoloop was placed at the base of the appendix. The appendix was transected using a laparoscopic stapler. The stump was inspected for hemostasis. The specimen was removed in a retrieval bag. The peritoneal cavity was irrigated with 3 liters of warm saline. The ports were removed under direct vision. Hemostasis was confirmed. No other abnormalities were noted in the bowel or other abdominal organs.

CLOSURE:
Skin incisions were closed with subcutaneous sutures and steri-strips. The patient tolerated the procedure well. Estimated blood loss was minimal. The patient was transferred to the recovery room in stable condition.

POSTOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS:  SYNOVIAL PANNUS, KNEE (J01.9)

FINDINGS AND COURSE OF OPERATION:
The patient was brought to the operating room and identified per standard protocol. Informed consent was verified. The patient was placed in the supine position. General anesthesia was administered by Dr. Samuel Kim. The right lower extremity was prepped and draped in the standard sterile fashion. A tourniquet was applied to the thigh and inflated to 250 mmHg.

Arthroscopic portals were established in the anterolateral and anteromedial positions. The joint was inspected. Significant synovial hypertrophy and pannus formation were noted throughout the suprapatellar pouch and the medial and lateral gutters. The articular cartilage of the femur and tibia was graded as Outerbridge Stage II. The menisci were intact and stable. The anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments were intact and functional.

A 4.0 mm shaver was introduced. The synovial tissue was resected systematically from the suprapatellar pouch, medial gutter, and lateral gutter. Care was taken to avoid injury to the patellar tendon and the meniscal attachments. Hemostasis was achieved with monopolar cautery. The joint was lavaged with normal saline.

The tourniquet was deflated. The portals were closed with steri-strips. A sterile compression dressing was applied. The patient tolerated the procedure well. No complications occurred. Estimated blood loss was 50 mL. The patient was extubated and transferred to the post-anesthesia care unit in stable condition.

SUBJECTIVE
Patient presents with right shoulder pain of 2 months duration. Pain is described as sharp and localized to the lateral aspect of the shoulder, exacerbated by overhead activities and abduction between 60-120 degrees (painful arc). Pain interferes with sleep, particularly when rolling onto the affected side. Patient reports working 10+ hours daily at a desk. No history of trauma. OBJECTIVE
Visual inspection: No significant swelling or erythema. Mild atrophy of the supraspinatus muscle noted.

ASSESSMENT

The patient exhibits classic signs of subacromial impingement, evidenced by the painful arc, positive impingement tests, and preserved passive range of motion. OPERATIVE REPORT

PATIENT: MOREL, LÉA
MRN: 882314
DATE OF BIRTH: 14/05/1987
AGE: 37
SEX: FEMALE
SURGEON: DR. ELIAS VOGEL
ASSISTANT: DR. CLAIRE BERNASCONI
ANESTHESIA: GENERAL ANESTHESIA BY DR. HENRI LACROIX
ANESTHESIA TYPE: GA
DATE OF OPERATION: 12/10/2023
HOSPITAL: HÔPITAL DU VALAIS, SION
SURGICAL PROCEDURE: LAPAROSCOPY, DIAGNOSTIC AND THERAPEUTIC; RIGHT OVARIAN CYSTECTOMY; APPENDICECTOMY
PREOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: RIGHT OVARIAN CYST, ACUTE APPENDICITIS
POSTOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: RIGHT OVARIAN CYST, ACUTE APPENDICITIS

FINDINGS:
1. PERITONEUM: Slight serous fluid in the pelvis. No signs of peritonitis.
2. APPENDIX: The appendix is erythematous, edematous, and thickened (1.5 cm diameter). The tip is gangrenous. No perforation is visible. The base of the appendix is inflamed.
3. RIGHT OVARY: A 5 cm cyst is present on the right ovary. The surface is smooth. The left ovary appears normal.
4. UTERUS: Normal in size and shape. No fibroids.
5. TUBES: Both fallopian tubes appear normal. No hydrosalpinx.

COURSE OF OPERATION:
The patient was prepped and draped in the standard sterile fashion. Pneumoperitoneum was established with a Veress needle at the umbilicus. A 10 mm port was placed at the umbilicus. Two additional 5 mm ports were placed in the right lower quadrant and the left lower quadrant under direct vision.

Exploration revealed a large right ovarian cyst and an inflamed appendix. The decision was made to proceed with both a right ovarian cystectomy and an appendectomy.

First, the appendix was isolated. The mesoappendix was divided using harmonic scissors. The base of the appendix was stapled using a 45 mm Endo-GIA stapler. The distal tip was ligated and divided. The specimen was placed in an endobag and extracted through the umbilical port.

Next, the right ovarian cyst was addressed. The cyst wall was incised with electrocautery. The cyst contents were aspirated. The cyst wall was dissected off the ovarian cortex using electrocautery and sharp dissection. The base of the cyst was coagulated to ensure hemostasis. The ovarian stroma was inspected and appeared healthy. The right ovary was preserved.

The abdomen was irrigated with warm saline. All hemostasis was secured. The ports were removed, and the skin incisions were closed with subcuticular sutures. Sterile dressings were applied.

The patient tolerated the procedure well and was transferred to the PACU in stable condition.

SPECIMEN: APPENDIX, RIGHT OVARIAN CYST
SEND TO: PATHOLOGY

dialogue:
[nurse] Good morning, this is Nurse Elara from the Zurich Psychiatric Outpatient Clinic, calling to follow up on your referral. Is this Mr. Kumar?
[patient] Yes, this is me. Good morning. My hearing is not what it used to be, so please speak a little slowly.
[nurse] Understood, Mr. Kumar. I will speak clearly. My name is Elara. We received a referral from Dr. Meier at Kantonsspital Zurich regarding your recent memory concerns.
[patient] Yes, Dr. Meier sent the letter. He is a good man, but I think he is too young to understand an old man's mind.
[nurse] I respect Dr. Meier's assessment. He noted that you have been having difficulty remembering recent events, which is different from normal aging. How have you been feeling lately?
[patient] I am tired. Very tired. I used to play badminton every Tuesday at the Ballyhalgo Sports Club, but now I forget to put on my shoes.
[nurse] I am sorry to hear that. Stopping a hobby you love can be very difficult. Can you tell me about your living situation? Are you living alone?
[patient] I live alone at 44 Seestrasse, 8002 Zurich. My neighbor, Mrs. Raj, is kind, but I do not want to burden her.
[nurse] Thank you for sharing that. Mrs. Raj sounds like a supportive neighbor. Do you have family nearby, or did you move from elsewhere?
[patient] I moved from Jaffna, Sri Lanka, forty years ago. I worked for twenty years at the textile mill in Winterthur. I am retired now.
[nurse] That is a long time in Switzerland. Do you still have contact with colleagues from the mill?
[patient] Yes, my old friend Suresh still calls on Sundays. He worries about me. He says I am losing my way.
[nurse] It is good that you have a friend like Suresh. Can you describe what is happening with your memory? Is it getting worse quickly or slowly?
[patient] It was slow. But last month, I walked into the kitchen and did not know what I was doing. I stood there for ten minutes.
[nurse] That sounds frightening. Did you feel confused about where you were at that moment?
[patient] I knew I was home, but I did not know why I was there. I felt like a stranger in my own house.
[nurse] I understand. Has this happened to you when you are out in public?
[patient] Yes. Last week, I went to the market in Zurich. I forgot to pay for the bread. The shopkeeper laughed at me. I was so ashamed.
[nurse] Shame is a very common feeling when memory slips occur. It is not your fault. The brain is changing.
[patient] My record number is 88421-A. I think Dr. Meier sent the papers under that number.
[nurse] Yes, I have that file open. We need to schedule an in-person appointment to assess your cognitive function more thoroughly.
[patient] Can I come on Thursday? I am usually free then.
[nurse] Let me check the schedule. We have an opening on Thursday, October 12th, at 10:30 AM. Does that work for you?
[patient] Yes, that is good. I will ask Mrs. Raj to drive me. Her car is reliable.
[nurse] That is a wonderful plan. Do you have any other symptoms? Any changes in mood or sleep?
[patient] I sleep too much. I sleep twelve hours a day. And I feel sad. Not crying sad, but empty sad.
[nurse] Low mood and excessive sleep are often associated with the cognitive changes we are discussing. Is there anything that makes you anxious?
[patient] I worry about my money. I am afraid I will forget to pay my bills and lose my apartment.
[nurse] That is a valid concern. We will discuss financial planning with a social worker during your admission.
[patient] Thank you. I just want to stay in my home in Zurich. I do not want to go to a nursing home.
[nurse] We will do our best to support you in your home for as long as possible. We will coordinate with Dr. Meier's team at Kantonsspital Zurich.
[patient] Yes. Please tell Dr. Meier I am ready to start the tests.
[nurse] I will note that. Do you have any questions for me before we hang up?
[patient] No. Please keep my phone number, 079-555-0192, in your system.
[nurse] It is already in the system. I will send a confirmation letter to your address at 44 Seestrasse, 8002 Zurich, tomorrow.
[patient] Thank you, Nurse Elara. Goodbye.
[nurse] Goodbye, Mr. Kumar. Take care of yourself until Thursday.

PATIENT NAME: Kumar, Rajendran
DATE OF BIRTH: 14/03/1939
AGE: 85
SEX: Male
MEDICAL RECORD NUMBER: 88421-A
DATE OF ADMISSION: 12/10/2024
REFERRING PHYSICIAN: Dr. Anna Meier, Kantonsspital Zurich
ADMITTING DIAGNOSIS: Suspected Major Neurocognitive Disorder due to Alzheimer's Disease

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Rajendran Kumar, an 85-year-old male, is admitted for further cognitive assessment and diagnostic clarification. He is a retired textile worker who has resided in Zurich for four decades after emigrating from Jaffna, Sri Lanka. His referring physician, Dr. Anna Meier of Kantonsspital Zurich, noted a progressive decline in memory and executive function over the past six months, accelerating in the last four weeks. The patient reports increasing difficulty with instrumental activities of daily living, specifically managing finances and meal preparation. He describes episodes of spatial disorientation, including standing in his kitchen without purpose and failing to pay for groceries at the local market. He reports associated symptoms of apathy, excessive daytime somnolence (sleeping 12+ hours), and mild depressive mood characterized by feelings of emptiness and shame. He lives alone at 44 Seestrasse, 8002 Zurich, and maintains limited social contact, primarily with his neighbor, Mrs. Raj, and a former colleague, Suresh, whom he speaks to weekly. He previously participated in badminton at the Ballyhalgo Sports Club but has ceased activity due to forgetfulness.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Hypertension (diagnosed 2015), managed with Amlodipine 5mg daily. No history of diabetes, stroke, or head trauma. No substance abuse history. No psychiatric history prior to the current presentation.

FAMILY HISTORY
No known history of dementia in parents or siblings. Brother passed away in 2018 from cardiac arrest.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Single, no children. Lived in Switzerland for 40 years. Worked for 20 years at the Winterthur Textile Mill. Currently retired. Lives independently.

MENTAL STATUS EXAMINATION
APPEARANCE: Well-groomed, dressed in clean casual attire. Appears older than stated age.
BEHAVIOR: Cooperative but slow to respond. Psychomotor slowing is evident.
ATTITUDE: Respectful and polite.
AFFECT: Restricted range. Described as "empty." No psychomotor agitation.
MOOD: "Sad," "Tired."
THOUGHT PROCESS: Linear and logical, though slow. No evidence of tangentiality or circumstantiality.
THOUGHT CONTENT: Preoccupied with fear of financial loss and loss of independence. Denies suicidal ideation. Denies hallucinations or delusions.
PERCEPTION: No auditory or visual hallucinations reported.
COGNITION:
Orientation: Oriented to person and place. Disoriented to time (states it is "last week").
Attention: 3/5 digits forward, 2/5 digits backward.
Memory: 0/3 items recalled after 5 minutes. No confabulation noted.
Language: Fluency intact. No aphasia. Good comprehension.
Visuospatial: Unable to copy intersecting pentagons correctly.
INSIGHT: Fair. Acknowledges memory problems but minimizes severity.
JUDGMENT: Impaired.

ASSESSMENT
Mr. Kumar presents with progressive cognitive decline affecting multiple domains, including memory, orientation, and executive function, consistent with Major Neurocognitive Disorder. The pattern of episodic memory loss and spatial disorientation raises high suspicion for Alzheimer's Disease. Comorbid depressive symptoms are present. The rapid decline in functional independence warrants inpatient observation for baseline cognitive testing, neuroimaging (MRI), and metabolic workup to rule out reversible causes.

PLAN
1. Admit to inpatient psychiatric unit for 72 hours.
2. Order MRI Brain without contrast.
3. Order comprehensive metabolic panel, CBC, TSH, Vitamin B12, and folate levels.
4. Administer MoCA and MMSE upon stabilization.
5. Initiate supportive care.
6. Contact Dr. Anna Meier at Kantonsspital Zurich with preliminary findings.
7. Social work to assess home safety and potential need for in-home assistance.

dialogue:
[nurse] Morning, David. I’m Sarah, from the home care team. How are you feeling this morning?
[patient] Not great, Sarah. The swelling in my legs is really bad. I couldn’t get the socks on without help.
[nurse] I can see that. Let’s have a look at your ankles. I need to check the skin integrity and measure the circumference.
[patient] It feels tight and itchy. I’ve been scratching it more than I should.
[nurse] I see some minor excoriations here. We need to be careful not to break the skin further. I’ll apply some emollient after I check your compression stockings.
[nurse_2] I’ve been reviewing the notes from your last visit on 12th October. Your blood pressure was quite elevated then.
[nurse] Yes, I remember. Dr. Evans adjusted his medication. Has he taken his new dose of Furosemide as prescribed?
[patient] I took it yesterday and today. I’ve been going to the loo a lot, though.
[nurse] That is expected initially. We need to monitor your fluid balance. Have you weighed yourself?
[patient] I tried, but the scales in the hallway are broken.
[nurse] No problem. I have a portable digital scale with me. Let’s do that now.
[nurse_2] The scale is working fine. Let’s get you on it.
[patient] 84 kilograms. It was 82 last week.
[nurse] A two-kilogram increase in one week suggests fluid retention. We need to report this to the GP immediately.
[nurse_2] I will call the practice. Do you have the direct number for Dr. Evans?
[patient] It’s on the fridge. 0131 456 7890.
[nurse] Thank you. I’ll give them a ring to discuss adjusting the diuretic dose. In the meantime, I will elevate your legs.
[nurse_2] I can help you with that. We can use the wedge pillows from your sister’s visit.
[patient] Oh, right. Claire sent those over last month. She’s in Edinburgh now, actually.
[nurse] Claire? Is she your sister?
[patient] Yes, my sister Claire, aged 38. She moved back to Edinburgh after working in London for years.
[nurse_2] It’s good to have family support. And your brother, James?
[patient] James is 44. He’s still in Manchester, just over the border. He checks in on me most evenings.
[nurse] That’s reassuring. Did he help with the physiotherapy exercises yesterday?
[patient] He did. He’s quite good at it. We used to go hiking together when we lived in Leeds.
[nurse] Leeds? I didn’t realize you moved from there.
[patient] We moved from Leeds to Glasgow about five years ago. I was born in Glasgow, actually, on 14th June 1983.
[nurse_2] Noted. So, local to the area. That makes coordination with the community health nurse easier.
[nurse] Speaking of which, I need to check your wound care plan. The ulcer on your left leg is still present, isn’t it?
[patient] It is. It’s smaller, but it weeps a bit.
[nurse] I will perform a compression bandage change. This is crucial for healing venous ulcers.
[nurse_2] I’ll prepare the sterile kit. Make sure to dispose of the old bandages in the clinical waste bag.
[patient] Is it going to hurt?
[nurse] It might be a little uncomfortable when we clean the wound, but we will be gentle.
[nurse_2] We have a local anesthetic spray if you prefer.
[patient] No, I can manage. I’ve had worse.
[nurse] Okay. I’m going to clean the area now.
[nurse_2] I’m applying the new compression layer. It’s important it’s not too tight.
[patient] It feels firm, but okay.
[nurse] Good. We need to ensure the circulation is intact. I’ll check your pedal pulses after dressing.
[nurse_2] The pulses are palpable. Capillary refill is under two seconds.
[nurse] Excellent. Now, let’s talk about your diet. Have you been watching your salt intake?
[patient] I try. I had chips yesterday, though.
[nurse] We need to limit sodium to help with the fluid retention. The diuretics will help, but diet is key.
[nurse_2] I’ve written down some low-sodium recipes from the dietitian.
[patient] Thanks. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, is actually a retired nurse. She gave me some advice.
[nurse] Mrs. Higgins? Is she in the next house?
[patient] Yes, number 42. She’s been very kind.
[nurse] It’s great to have that community support.
[nurse_2] I’m going to check your blood pressure again now that we’ve changed the dressing.
[nurse] The BP is 145/90. Still a bit high.
[nurse_2] We will mention this to Dr. Evans. He may need to adjust the beta-blocker.
[patient] I feel a bit dizzy when I stand up quickly.
[nurse] That’s orthostatic hypotension. Be careful. Stand up slowly.
[nurse_2] I’ll leave a fall prevention checklist in your kitchen.
[nurse] Also, remind me, when is your next follow-up appointment?
[patient] It’s in three weeks. 24th November.
[nurse] I will book the next home visit for 27th November to check on the wound progress.
[nurse_2] I will send the referral to the community team.
[nurse] Do you have any questions before we go?
[patient] Just that I’m worried about the swelling.
[nurse] We are monitoring it closely. If it gets much worse, or if you have chest pain, call 999 immediately.
[nurse_2] We are here to help. Your family is in the loop, and we are coordinating with the GP.
[patient] Thank you, Sarah and... what was your name again?
[nurse_2] I’m Emily.
[patient] Thank you, Emily. And Sarah.
[nurse] Take care, David. Rest well.
[nurse_2] See you next week.

PATIENT: Dubois, Claire
AGE: 41

PRE-OP DIAGNOSIS: Full-thickness rotator cuff tear, left shoulder
POST-OP DIAGNOSIS: Full-thickness rotator cuff tear, left shoulder
PROCEDURE: Arthroscopic rotator cuff repair, left shoulder

FINDINGS:
The patient was prepped and draped in the standard sterile fashion. A standard posterior shoulder arthroscopy was performed. Upon entering the joint, the subacromial space was evaluated. A full-thickness tear of the supraspinatus tendon measuring approximately 2.5 cm in diameter was identified. The tear extended to the bursal and articular surfaces. The remaining tendon edges were healthy but retracted. The subacromial space showed mild impingement changes. The rotator cuff was repaired using two suture anchors placed in the greater tuberosity. The tendon was reattached to the bone using a double-row technique. The joint was lavaged and closed.

COURSE OF OPERATION:
The patient tolerated the procedure well. Estimated blood loss was minimal. There were no intraoperative complications. The patient was taken to the recovery room in stable condition.

OPERATIVE REPORT

PATIENT: Tesfay, Solomon
MRN: 99-882-12
AGE: 89
SEX: M
DATE OF BIRTH: 14/05/1935
SURGEON: Dr. Elias Keller
ASSISTANTS: Dr. Mira Voss, RN. Sarah Lind
ANESTHESIA: General Endotracheal Anesthesia
ANESTHESIOLOGIST: Dr. Paul Reuter
DATE OF OPERATION: 18/03/2024
OPERATING ROOM: 4
SURGICAL TECHNICIAN: M. Weber

PREOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS:
Displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture, right hip.

POSTOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS:
Same as above.

PROCEDURE:
Right Total Hip Arthroplasty, posterior approach.

INDICATIONS:
The patient is an 89-year-old male with a displaced femoral neck fracture sustained on 12/03/2024. Conservative management is contraindicated due to displacement and patient age. Total hip arthroplasty is indicated to restore function and relieve pain.

FINDINGS:
The right hip was approached via a standard posterior approach. The skin was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion. A 15 cm incision was made over the greater trochanter. Subcutaneous tissues and fascia were incised in line with the skin incision. The short external rotators were identified and released. The posterior capsule was incised in a T-shape. The femoral head was dislocated. The fracture was confirmed to be displaced. The femoral neck was removed. The acetabulum was prepared with reamers to size 54 mm. A cementless acetabular cup was implanted using press-fit technique. A 2 mm offset was achieved. The femur was prepared with reamers and broaches to size 14 mm. A 14 mm, 4 mm offset femoral stem was implanted with cementless fixation. A 36 mm modular femoral head was attached. The hip was reduced. Stability was checked in flexion, extension, abduction, and rotation. The short external rotators were reattached with non-absorbable sutures. The capsule was repaired. The fascia was closed with absorbable sutures. The subcutaneous tissue was closed with absorbable sutures. The skin was closed with subcuticular sutures and Steri-Strips. A sterile dressing was applied.

COURSE:
The patient tolerated the procedure well. Estimated blood loss was 300 ml. No transfusion was required. The patient was extubated in the operating room and transferred to the PACU in stable condition.

The purulent fluid was suctioned and irrigated copiously with warm saline. The base of the appendix was identified. A laparoscopic stapler was applied across the base of the appendix, ensuring healthy tissue margins. The appendix was divided and retrieved in an endobag through the umbilical port. The staple line was inspected and was hemostatic. The peritoneal cavity was re-irrigated to clear any remaining debris. The ports were removed under direct vision, and the fascial defects were closed with 3-0 polydioxanone sutures. The skin was closed with Steri-Strips. Hemostasis was excellent. The patient tolerated the procedure well and was extubated in the operating room.

DISPOSITION:
The patient was transferred to the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU) in stable condition.

[pharmacist] good morning , mr . yilmaz . i see you have a new prescription for warfarin from dr . weber . can you tell me a little about your recent travel ?

[patient] i have been experiencing some swelling in my left leg and mild pain when i walk . dr . weber referred me to the surgical department for a scan .
[pharmacist] that is consistent with a deep vein thrombosis . this medication , warfarin , is a blood thinner . it will help prevent the clot from growing or moving .
[patient] i am a bit worried . my brother , demir , has a similar condition called pulmonary embolism . he says it is very dangerous .
[pharmacist] i understand your concern . your brother demir’s case was serious , but your situation is being managed proactively . the goal is to keep your blood thin enough to prevent clots but not so thin that you bleed .
[patient] i am sixty years old , so i am not as quick to recover . i work as a structural engineer for kaeler construction group in munich . i am on my feet a lot .
[pharmacist] at sixty , your body does process medication differently than when you were younger . you will need regular blood tests , called inr checks , to adjust the dose .
[patient] how often do i need to go to the lab ?
[pharmacist] initially , every few days until your levels are stable . then , maybe once a month . it is important to keep these appointments with dr . weber’s team at st. anna hospital .
[patient] dr . weber is very thorough . he explained that i need to be careful with what i eat .
[pharmacist] yes . vitamin k is in leafy greens like spinach and kale . it counteracts the warfarin . you do not need to stop eating them , but you must keep your intake consistent .
[patient] i love turkish food . there is a lot of parsley and dill . will that be a problem ?
[pharmacist] parsley and dill contain vitamin k , but in smaller amounts than spinach . just do not suddenly double your portion of salad if you have been eating little . consistency is key .
[patient] and alcohol ? i have a glass of wine sometimes .
[pharmacist] alcohol can affect how your liver processes warfarin . heavy drinking can increase the bleeding risk . one glass of wine occasionally is usually fine , but do not binge drink .
[patient] what about painkillers ? i might need something for the leg pain .

[patient] i will be careful . i have a lot of responsibility at kaeler construction , so i do not want to be hospitalized .

[patient] no , i think i am clear . thank you .

1. Initiate a rehabilitation program focusing on pain management, range of motion restoration, and quadriceps strengthening.

4. Follow-up appointment scheduled for 28 October 2024 to reassess progress.
5. We will continue to monitor for any signs of meniscal tear requiring further imaging or orthopedic consultation.

Please do not hesitate to contact us if you have any concerns or require additional information.

Sincerely,

Sarah Miller, DPT

dialogue:
[pharmacist] Good morning, Mr. Garcia. I am Maria, your community pharmacist. I have your new prescription from Dr. Keller here at the clinic.
[patient] Morning. Thank you. I was waiting for this package.
[pharmacist] It is for your hypertension, correct? The doctor prescribed Amlodipine 5 mg, once daily.
[patient] Yes. I have been feeling a bit dizzy lately, especially when I stand up quickly.
[pharmacist] That is a common side effect of blood pressure medication, but also a sign that we need to monitor your pressure closely. Did you have any dizziness on your recent trip to Zurich?
[patient] Actually, I traveled to Barcelona last week to visit my sister. I noticed it there too, but I thought it was the jet lag.
[pharmacist] No jet lag to Barcelona, but the travel stress can definitely raise your blood pressure. How are you managing your work schedule?
[patient] I am the Operations Manager at Helvetia Logistics. It is quite demanding right now with the new warehouse expansion.
[pharmacist] That sounds stressful. Have you been able to eat regularly? Salt intake can interfere with how well this medication works.
[patient] I try to, but I often skip lunch when I am on the floor checking inventory.
[pharmacist] Skipping meals can lead to spikes in blood pressure. This pill helps relax your blood vessels, so it needs a consistent routine. Do you take any other supplements?
[patient] No, just the vitamins my wife gives me.
[pharmacist] Good. One important thing: do not crush or chew this tablet. Swallow it whole with a glass of water.
[patient] Understood. Can I take it with food?
[pharmacist] Yes, you can take it with or without food. Just try to take it at the same time every day. Morning is usually best for Amlodipine.
[patient] I usually wake up at 6:00. I will take it right after I brush my teeth.
[pharmacist] Perfect. Now, let us discuss side effects. You might experience swelling in your ankles or feet. This is called peripheral edema.
[patient] Is that serious?
[pharmacist] It is not dangerous, but you should report it if it becomes severe or if you gain more than 2 kg in a week. Also, you might feel flushed or have a headache.
[patient] I have had headaches before. How do I know if it is the medicine?
[pharmacist] If the headache is mild, it may subside after a few days. If it is severe or persistent, call Dr. Keller. Here is his direct line: 044 882 10 20.
[patient] I will write that down. I am not very good with these numbers.
[pharmacist] No problem. I have also sent an email summary to your address, g.mendez@helvetialogistics.ch, with the dosage instructions.
[patient] Ah, I missed that. I am always on my phone for work emails.
[pharmacist] That is fine. Just double-check the inbox. Also, avoid excessive grapefruit juice. It can increase the levels of the drug in your blood.
[patient] I do drink a lot of orange juice, but rarely grapefruit.
[pharmacist] Good. Just to be safe, try to limit it. Do you have any questions about the cost or insurance?
[patient] My employer covers most of it, but I need to know the co-payment.
[pharmacist] With your LAMal insurance, the co-payment is 10% of the price, up to a maximum of CHF 25 per pack.
[patient] That is manageable.
[pharmacist] You can pay here or by invoice. Since you are in a hurry, I will print the receipt for your expense report.
[patient] Thank you, Maria. This is very helpful.
[pharmacist] You are welcome. Remember, if you feel faint or have chest pain, go to the emergency room immediately. Do not wait.
[patient] I will be careful. I really appreciate your patience.
[pharmacist] Take care, Mr. Garcia. Stay hydrated and keep an eye on your ankles.
[patient] I will. Have a nice day.
[pharmacist] Goodbye.

OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS:
SEVERE OSTEOARTHRITIS, RIGHT KNEE

FINDINGS:
The right knee was inspected and found to have advanced osteoarthritic changes involving the medial and lateral compartments. There was significant loss of articular cartilage, subchondral sclerosis, and osteophyte formation. The anterior cruciate ligament was intact but attenuated. The posterior cruciate ligament was also intact. No signs of infection or malignancy were noted.

COURSE OF OPERATION:
The patient was placed in the supine position. The right lower extremity was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion. A tourniquet was inflated to 250 mmHg. A medial parapatellar arthrotomy was performed. The patella was everted. Extensive debridement of osteophytes was carried out. The femoral, tibial, and patellar surfaces were resected using a computer-assisted navigation system to ensure proper alignment.

A cemented posterior-stabilized total knee prosthesis was implanted. The components were seated securely with polymethylmethacrylate cement. The joint was irrigated copiously with warm saline. The extensor mechanism was tested, and full passive flexion and extension were achieved. The arthrotomy was closed in layers with absorbable sutures. The skin was closed with staples. A sterile dressing was applied. The tourniquet was deflated, and hemostasis was confirmed.

The patient tolerated the procedure well. Estimated blood loss was 400 mL. Two units of packed red blood cells were transfused intraoperatively due to a drop in hemoglobin. The patient was extubated in the operating room and transferred to the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit in stable condition.

E. VANCE, M.D.

FINDINGS:
The patient was placed in the supine position. The left lower extremity was prepped and draped in the standard sterile fashion. A lateral approach was utilized. The incision was made along the lateral aspect of the hip. The muscles were retracted to expose the greater trochanter and the femoral neck. The femoral neck was osteotomized and removed. The femoral head was dislocated and removed. The acetabulum was exposed. The acetabular cartilage was diseased and removed using a reamer. The acetabular cup was implanted and secured with cement. The femoral canal was reamed. A cemented femoral stem was inserted and secured. The hip was reduced, and stability was confirmed through range of motion. The wound was irrigated, layered closure was performed, and a sterile dressing was applied.

COURSE OF OPERATION:
The patient tolerated the procedure well. Estimated blood loss was 300 mL. No intraoperative complications were noted. The patient was extubated in the operating room and transferred to the post-anesthesia care unit in stable condition. Post-operative orders included DVT prophylaxis with apixaban, pain management with paracetamol and opioids as needed, and physical therapy. The patient was instructed to follow weight-bearing restrictions as per the surgical protocol.

dialogue:
[pharmacist] Good afternoon, Mr. Solano. I see you are here for your new prescription for the blood pressure medication we discussed with Dr. Weber.
[patient] Yes, good afternoon. I am a bit worried because I have been feeling very tired lately, and the doctor said I need to start this new pill.
[pharmacist] I understand. Fatigue can sometimes happen when we adjust our heart’s workload. This new medication, Amlodipine 5 mg, helps relax your blood vessels so your heart doesn't have to pump as hard.
[patient] I was actually just back from my trip to Seville last week. The heat and the walking around the plazas really took it out of me.
[pharmacist] Seville is beautiful, but it is certainly intense in the summer. It is good that you rested when you returned to Basel. Have you been taking any other painkillers for the tiredness?
[patient] No, mostly just plenty of water. I am a member of the FC Basel 1893 supporters club, and we were planning a weekend trip to Zurich for the derby, but I am canceling that now.
[pharmacist] That is a wise decision. Physical exertion while your blood pressure is unstable can be risky. Did Dr. Weber mention anything about when to take the first dose?
[patient] She said it was in the morning, but I am a night owl. Can I take it at night?
[pharmacist] For Amlodipine, it doesn't matter much whether it is morning or night, as long as you are consistent. However, since you tend to sleep later, taking it in the evening might help if you notice any swelling in your ankles, which is a common side effect.
[patient] Swelling in my ankles? I have noticed that before, especially after long days at the factory.
[pharmacist] Yes, peripheral edema is possible. It is usually mild. If it becomes severe or painful, you should contact us immediately. But generally, it is manageable.
[patient] I am sixty years old now, so I feel like my body is just slowing down. Is this a lifelong medication?
[pharmacist] It is likely a long-term treatment, Mr. Solano. Your blood pressure readings at the clinic were consistently high, which increases the risk of stroke or heart attack. This medication protects you from those events.
[patient] I see. So, how many pills a day?
[pharmacist] Just one tablet, once daily. You will find it in a blister pack. Here is your first month's supply.
[patient] Thank you. And what if I forget to take it?
[pharmacist] If you remember on the same day, take it as soon as you remember. If you only remember the next day, skip the missed dose and take the next one at your regular time. Do not double up.
[patient] Understood. Is there any food I should avoid?
[pharmacist] You should limit your intake of grapefruit and grapefruit juice. It can interact with the medication and cause the levels in your blood to rise too high.
[patient] I actually love grapefruit juice in the morning with my toast. That is a pity.
[pharmacist] It is just a small interaction, but to be safe, I would suggest sticking to orange or apple juice for now. We can review this in three months when we check your blood work.
[patient] Okay, no grapefruit. That is manageable. What about alcohol? I usually have a glass of wine after dinner.
[pharmacist] Moderate alcohol consumption is generally fine, but too much can lower your blood pressure further and cause dizziness. Stick to one or two glasses max.
[patient] I will be careful. I want to be fit enough to keep playing football with the club, even if I am just in the reserves now.
[pharmacist] That is a great goal. Keeping active is part of the treatment, but you must listen to your body. If you feel lightheaded, stop and rest.
[patient] And if I feel dizzy, what should I do?
[pharmacist] Sit or lie down immediately to prevent falling. If the dizziness persists or you feel chest pain, call emergency services.
[patient] I will keep that in mind. My record number is 8842-B, in case I need to reference it when I call.
[pharmacist] Noted. Dr. Weber at the University Hospital Basel will be monitoring your progress. Please make sure to keep your follow-up appointment in six weeks.
[patient] I have it in my calendar. Thank you for your help. It feels less scary now that I know what to expect.
[pharmacist] You are welcome. This is a common condition, and with the right management, you can live a very active life. Do you have any other questions?
[patient] No, that was very helpful. I appreciate your patience.
[pharmacist] Take care, Mr. Solano. Stay safe and stay hydrated, especially with the weather changing.

ASSISTANTS: DR. ELMIRA HASSAN, NURSE ANESTHETIST: K. STEINER

PRE-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) of the Right Lower Extremity
POST-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) of the Right Lower Extremity

PROCEDURE: Right Lower Extremity Venous Duplex Ultrasound with Compression
ANESTHESIA: Local (None required)

FINDINGS:
The patient is an 81-year-old male, retired engineer formerly employed by Siemens AG, who resides in Vienna. He recently relocated from Graz and presents with acute onset swelling and erythema of the right calf. He reports a recent long-distance train travel to Salzburg. He is an active participant in the tennis club "Verein Währing 1905" and his neighbor, Herr Kowalski, accompanied him to the facility. The patient has no prior history of venous thromboembolism and is not currently on anticoagulation therapy.

COURSE OF OPERATION:
The patient was placed in the supine position. The right lower extremity was exposed. A linear high-frequency ultrasound probe was used to visualize the common femoral vein, superficial femoral vein, popliteal vein, and calf veins. Compression was applied sequentially.

In the proximal thigh, the common femoral vein and superficial femoral vein were compressible with no evidence of thrombus. In the popliteal fossa, a non-compressible, echogenic thrombus was identified in the popliteal vein, extending approximately 4 cm distally. The thrombus appears acute to subacute based on echogenicity and lack of significant retraction. Distal extension into the gastrocnemius veins was noted. The left lower extremity was also scanned and showed no evidence of DVT.

No intervention was performed as the procedure was diagnostic. The skin was cleaned and dry. The patient tolerated the procedure well and was discharged to the waiting area for further management by Dr. Schneider.

The patient is a 55-year-old Kosovar Albanian woman presenting with a 3-week history of worsening insomnia, anxiety, and diurnal fatigue. She reports difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep, frequently waking at 03:00-04:00 with intrusive thoughts. She describes chest tightness associated with anxiety, which resolves with slow breathing. She works as a receptionist for Hotel Alpenrose and has taken two sick days this week due to functional impairment. She lives with her brother, Besnik (age 58), who provides social support. Her daughter, Lila (age 28), resides in Bern. The patient previously engaged in social activities, specifically knitting at the Wollisfelser Handarbeitsgruppe in Wollishofen, but has ceased attending due to fatigue and driving anxiety.

PAST PSYCHIATRIC HISTORY
Diagnosed with Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) in 2019. Previous hospitalizations: None.
Previous outpatient visits:
- 12.01.2024: Follow-up with Dr. Keller; medication adjusted.
- 05.02.2024: Laboratory blood work (CMP, Thyroid panel) ordered; results pending.

MEDICAL HISTORY
Hypertension (stable). No history of cardiac arrhythmia.
Surgical History: None.

CURRENT MEDICATIONS
Sertraline 100 mg PO daily
Clonazepam 0.5 mg PO qhs
Amlodipine 5 mg PO daily

ALLERGIES
NKDA (No Known Drug Allergies)

MENTAL STATUS EXAMINATION
Appearance: Well-groomed, dressed in modest professional attire.
Behavior: Cooperative, mild psychomotor agitation observed (picking at fingernails).
Speech: Normal rate, volume, and rhythm.
Mood: "Anxious," "Tired."
Affect: Anxious, restricted range, congruent with mood.
Thought Process: Linear, logical, goal-directed.
Thought Content: Preoccupied with sleep and work performance. Denies suicidal or homicidal ideation. Denies hallucinations. No evidence of paranoia.
Perception: No auditory or visual hallucinations elicited.
Cognition: Alert and oriented x4 (person, place, time, situation). Attention and concentration intact (7 backwards from 20).
Insight: Good; recognizes symptoms as related to anxiety.
Judgment: Intact.

ASSESSMENT
55-year-old female with history of GAD presenting with exacerbation of anxiety and insomnia. Functional impairment at work and cessation of social hobbies. Current regimen inadequate for symptom control. Rule out secondary causes of insomnia (thyroid, sleep apnea) pending lab results from 05.02.2024.

PLAN
1. Continue Sertraline 100 mg daily.
2. Increase Clonazepam to 1.0 mg qhs for 2 weeks, then taper.
3. Refer to sleep study if insomnia persists after medication adjustment.
4. Encourage resumption of social activities (knitting group) when energy levels improve.
5. Follow-up in 2 weeks (29.03.2024).
6. Patient provided with crisis resource card (143).

[pharmacist] good morning , ms . weber . i see dr . keller sent over a new prescription for you . is this the first time you are picking this up ?

[patient] that makes sense . i usually have coffee and a croissant at the bakery near my apartment in the mitte district .
[pharmacist] perfect . now , are you currently taking any other medications or supplements ?
[patient] i take vitamin d drops in the winter , and sometimes ibuprofen for headaches .
[pharmacist] ibuprofen is fine in small amounts , but just be aware that combining ssris with nsaids can slightly increase the risk of stomach bleeding .
[patient] i will keep that in mind . i try to use it rarely anyway .
[pharmacist] good . what about alcohol ?

[pharmacist] that is generally acceptable , but i would advise limiting it to one standard drink and watching how you feel .
[patient] okay . my colleague , sarah , actually told me that her husband took this for years and it changed his life .

[pharmacist] it is a journey . it can take two to four weeks to feel the full benefit .
[patient] so i should not expect to feel better immediately ?
